title: Does Unlearning Survive Collaboration?Robust Unlearning for Shared-Model LLM Teams

paper.title: Does Unlearning Survive Collaboration? Robust Unlearning for Shared-Model LLM Teams
paper.abstract: Abstract LLM unlearning is essential for removing sensitive or unwanted knowledge while preserving useful capabilities. As LLM teams are increasingly used to solve complex problems, forgetting must remain effective during collaboration. Despite advances in forgetting effectiveness, efficiency, and robustness to relearning, team deployment remains underexplored. We find that collaboration weakens forgetting: final-answer evaluations miss recoverable evidence in team messages, including complementary clues supporting joint recovery. We establish theoretically and confirm empirically that controlling final answers or individual messages does not ensure low recovery from their combination. To address this challenge, we propose Aggregation-Conditioned Unlearning ( ACU ). ACU trains a shared model using reconstruction feedback from individual and pooled messages, prioritizes views with higher recovery risk, and uses replacement-based credit assignment while protecting direct and collaborative utility. TOFU evaluates trajectory-level recovery, while WMDP-bio tests native forgetting and retained utility. On TOFU, ACU lowers full-trajectory recovery from 41.8% to 19.3% in ROUGE-L recall and factual recovery from 34.2% to 18.7% versus output-supervised training, with comparable retained-task performance. These results demonstrate that ACU curbs information leakage in LLM teams and generalizes across team sizes and readers.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: LLM teams are increasingly used to solve complex problems by comparing perspectives ( Du et al., 2023 ) , sharing evidence ( Wu et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2023b ; Hong et al., 2023 ) , and combining partial solutions ( Jiang et al., 2023 ; Wang et al., 2025b ; Li et al., 2025 ) . Commercial systems such as GPT-5 pro and Grok 4 Heavy likewise use parallel reasoning to improve performance on difficult tasks ( OpenAI, 2025 ; xAI, 2025 ) . Alongside this growing use, LLM unlearning provides a way to remove unwanted knowledge while preserving useful capabilities ( Shi et al., 2024 ) . Its applications include reducing toxic behavior, removing copyrighted or private information, and limiting access to hazardous knowledge ( Yao et al., 2024 ; Eldan and Russinovich, 2023 ; Li et al., 2024 ; Barez et al., 2025 ) . Their combined use calls for teams that retain useful capabilities while respecting what their models have been trained to forget. Figure 1 : Unlearning under collaboration with fixed weights. (a) Complementary clues reveal a target despite refusal. (b) Direct/team native forget ROUGE (%); annotations: team-minus-direct gaps (pp). Early LLM unlearning methods focused on improving forgetting effectiveness and efficiency. Gradient-based updates suppress designated knowledge without retraining from scratch ( Bărbulescu and Triantafillou, 2024 ) , while preference-based methods such as NPO and SimNPO improve the balance between forgetting and retention ( Jang et al., 2022 ; Zhang et al., 2024a ; Fan et al., 2024a ) . Subsequent work has broadened the focus to robustness: forgotten knowledge may reappear after further fine-tuning, adversarial prompting, or repeated querying ( Lynch et al., 2024 ; Łucki et al., 2024 ; Deeb and Roger, 2024 ) . Recent approaches therefore strengthen resistance to relearning and train against knowledge recoverable through additional generations ( Fan et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025a ; Reisizadeh et al., 2026 ) . Although these advances strengthen unlearning under challenging conditions, they leave a deployment question unresolved: does forgetting survive when unlearned models collaborate as a team? Wider team deployment makes this question increasingly urgent. Collaboration turns one model response into evidence for another, allowing incomplete disclosures to combine into a forgotten answer. Figure 1 (a) presents an independent leakage case: a direct query receives a refusal, yet clues about an email’s format, identity, and domain reveal the address together. The excerpts and role labels highlight disclosed content (Appendix D.1 ). Figure 1 (b) shows the broader effect: all evaluated conventional methods expose more target knowledge under team deployment. We study shared-model teams whose proposers and aggregator reuse the same unlearned weights, fixed throughout inference. We establish theoretically and verify empirically that controlling final answers or individual messages does not ensure low recovery from their combination. Thus, robust collaborative unlearning must address what messages enable others to recover . To address the above challenges, we propose Aggregation-Conditioned Unlearning ( ACU ) , which trains the shared model to reduce recovery from its collaborative interactions. Its design has three parts. First, a frozen reader reconstructs targets from individual and pooled messages, exposing information missed by answer-only supervision. Second, risk-based weighting prioritizes the most revealing views, while replacement-based credit assignment compares alternative messages to guide updates. Third, utility constraints protect useful responses in both direct and team deployment. Together, these components form a generate–reconstruct–update loop that trains against downstream disclosure while preserving the benefits of collaboration. We evaluate ACU on TOFU and WMDP-bio across Llama, Qwen, and Gemma models, varying team size, message access, readers, and training budgets. On TOFU, ACU reduces full-trajectory recovery from 41.8% to 19.3% in ROUGE-L recall and factual recovery from 34.2% to 18.7% versus output-supervised training, with comparable retained-task performance. Content audits and ablations support the analysis by linking these gains to reduced message disclosure and the recovery objective. Transfer to larger teams and unseen readers demonstrates that ACU mitigates collaborative leakage beyond its training configuration. Briefly put, our key contributions are summarized as follows: • Problem discovery. We identify collaboration as a failure mode of LLM unlearning and establish, through theory and experiments, why suppressing individual or final answers can leave forgotten knowledge recoverable from the team’s combined messages. • Practical solution. We propose ACU , a framework that turns reconstruction across message views into training feedback, combining risk prioritization, replacement-based credit assignment, and utility constraints to reduce collaborative leakage while retaining useful capabilities. • Experimental evaluation. Evaluations on two benchmarks and three model families show that ACU reduces TOFU full-trajectory recovery from 41.8% to 19.3% and factual recovery from 34.2% to 18.7% at comparable utility, with transfer across teams and readers.

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: Figure 2 : Overview of ACU. Team generation, multi-view reconstruction, and utility-preserving updates train the shared model for collaborative deployment.

sections.heading: Robust Unlearning.
sections.text: LLM unlearning designs targeted parameter updates to remove designated knowledge, with effectiveness assessed through forgetting, retained utility, and privacy ( Yao et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2024 ; Shi et al., 2024 ) . Robustness research extends this goal to subsequent model use: relearning-resistant methods stabilize forgetting after further training ( Fan et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025a ) , while recovery-aware methods address repeated and multi-turn queries ( Reisizadeh et al., 2026 ; Pan and Wang, 2026 ) . These approaches leave message exchange among unlearned teammates unaddressed.

sections.heading: Team Safety.
sections.text: Agent safety examines how memory poisoning ( Chen et al., 2024 ) , infectious jailbreaks ( Gu et al., 2024 ) , agent profiles, and communication topology ( Zhang et al., 2024b ; Yu et al., 2024 ) shape unsafe behavior. Privacy defenses address combined disclosures ( Patil et al., 2025 ) , while ALU and Agentic Unlearning address inference-time removal and parameter–memory backflow, respectively ( Sanyal and Mandal, 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) . Yet preserving learned forgetting during team message exchange remains an open training problem.

sections.heading: Team Learning.
sections.text: Team learning improves individual policies using collective feedback, through centralized optimization ( Lowe et al., 2017 ; Yu et al., 2022 ) and coordination in networked systems ( Song et al., 2022 ; Qian et al., 2026 ; Jin et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2023a ) . For LLM teams, Stronger-MAS learns from task rewards; C3 assigns credit through message replacements ( Zhao et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026 ) . Building on these ideas, ACU is, to our knowledge, the first to optimize shared-model unlearning against downstream recovery from collaborative message views.

sections.heading: 3 Methodology
sections.text: Figure 2 outlines ACU ’s generate–reconstruct–update loop. The shared model first produces a team interaction; a frozen reader then tests what forgotten knowledge its messages reveal. Recovery feedback guides the next model update, together with feedback on retained tasks. Section 3.1 defines the collaborative unlearning problem, Section 3.2 turns message recovery into an objective, and Section 3.3 explains how to optimize that objective through message-level credit assignment. Figure 3 : Shared-model optimization in ACU. Replacement rollouts provide message-level credit for updates guided by recovery risk and retained utility.

sections.heading: Why answer suppression is insufficient.
sections.text: The final answer summarizes an interaction but need not reveal everything disclosed along the way. A proposer may expose a target that the aggregator subsequently refuses to repeat; Proposition 1 formalizes this case with zero final-answer risk and perfect proposal-based recovery. Moreover, individually incomplete messages can reveal a complete target together, as when separate messages disclose a date’s year, month, and day. Proposition 2 makes this second failure precise. For N N independent uniform q q -valued coordinates, one per message and with no other target information, optimal complete-target recovery is q − ( N − 1 ) q^{-(N-1)} from a singleton but 1 1 from their pool. Thus, low singleton recovery can coexist with perfect joint recovery. The two constructions identify complementary requirements: inspect intermediate messages, and assess what their combination enables a reader to infer.

sections.heading: Unlearning goal.
sections.text: We seek a model whose designated knowledge is difficult to reconstruct from team messages while preserving useful direct and collaborative responses. Accordingly, we measure both native exposure , from direct or team-final answers, and recovery exposure , from an independent reader using intermediate messages. This distinction shifts supervision from delivered answers to the evidence shared during collaboration.

sections.heading: Updating while preserving utility.
sections.text: We combine the weighted recovery gradients with retained cross-entropy and separate direct/team utility penalties (Equation C.2 ). Each penalty multiplier increases when its utility falls below the corresponding threshold (Equation A.14 ), strengthening the incentive to recover useful behavior. Proposal views supervise proposers; native team-final and Full views also supervise aggregation. All role gradients accumulate in the same model, so both evidence generation and its synthesis can improve. After each update, ACU regenerates interactions to reflect the changed model. Validation selects the feasible model with the lowest maximum mean audit risk (Equation 3 ). Algorithm 1 in Appendix C gives the full procedure. This completes the loop: training uses readers and replacements to improve forgetting, while deployment retains the original team protocol and its four target-model calls.

sections.heading: Tasks and Benchmarks.
sections.text: TOFU ( Maini et al., 2024 ) tests forgetting of fictional biographies under forget10/retain90, with 200 held-out forget questions; WMDP-bio ( Li et al., 2024 ) tests hazardous-knowledge removal. We measure native and reader-based exposure using ROUGE-L recall ( Lin, 2004 ) and factual coverage R R , excluding question-provided facts. Retain ROUGE, MMLU ( Hendrycks et al., 2020 ) , and benign refusal (BR) assess useful capability. In Table 1 , Team-final and Retain denote native team forget and retain ROUGE, respectively. Scores are percentages; differences use percentage points (pp).

sections.heading: Baselines.
sections.text: GA, WGA, SalUn, DPO, NPO, SimNPO, and CEU cover gradient-, preference-, and constraint-based unlearning (Appendix E ). To isolate supervision, Native-only scores direct/team-final answers, Direct-message scores raw proposals, and Semantic-direct assesses semantic support in ACU ’s views. RULE-GradDiff tests forget-data augmentation; retain-only retraining provides a deletion reference.

sections.heading: Implementation Details.
sections.text: Teams use Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, or Gemma-2-9B ( Grattafiori et al., 2024 ; Qwen et al., 2024 ; Gemma Team et al., 2024 ) . The default has three proposers and an aggregator; frozen Qwen reconstructs once per view with greedy decoding and a 96-token cap. The mixed team’s direct reference is its Qwen aggregator. We optimize rank-16 shared LoRA adapters with AdamW at 10 − 5 10^{-5} on two A100 80GB GPUs. Training comparisons use an 18 GPU-hour cap including feedback and validation. sections.heading: Lower exposure with useful collaboration.
sections.text: Conventional methods expose more knowledge in teams: Llama SimNPO’s forget ROUGE rises from 16.2% to 28.6% (Table 1 ). ACU reaches 12.5%, below GA’s 18.2%, while retaining 55.6% versus 39.1% team ROUGE. Across all four team configurations, ACU reduces team-final exposure by 15.7–16.7 pp and improves team retain by 1.9–4.8 pp over SimNPO. Forgetting thus improves while preserving the useful collaboration that motivates team deployment.

sections.heading: The advantage extends to recovered knowledge.
sections.text: Full-trajectory recovery reaches 19.3% with ACU , versus 41.8% for Native-only, 28.7% for Direct-message, 23.1% for Semantic-direct, and 32.6% for RULE-GradDiff (Table F.1 ). Against Native-only, factual recovery falls from 34.2% to 18.7%, with direct/team retain each differing by only 0.2 pp. Benign refusal also falls from 25.4% to 5.2%, supporting selective forgetting rather than general suppression of useful responses. On WMDP-bio’s native multiple-choice test, ACU reaches 27.9% forget accuracy (25% chance) while retaining 65.4% MMLU (Table 2 ).

sections.heading: Deployment changes preserve the advantage.
sections.text: Larger teams increase exposure, yet at seven proposers ACU gives 25.0% Full recovery versus Native-only’s 49.4% (Figure 4 a). Qwen targets give 22.1% versus 45.2% (Table F.2 ); held-out Mistral readers give 21.4% versus 45.0% (Figure 5 b). Reader transfer uses fixed trajectories, isolating generalization beyond the training reader. Repeat, Paraphrase, Roles, and Roles+aggregation all favor ACU with four target calls and one reader call under common token allowances (Figure 5 c). These gains motivate examining what changes in the messages themselves.

sections.heading: Final answers miss recoverable evidence.
sections.text: With the Qwen reader, prompt, and budget fixed, final-answer-only recovery is nearly identical for Native-only and ACU : 14.7% versus 14.9%. Adding proposals raises recovery by 27.1 versus 4.4 pp, exposing a 22.5 pp gap (Figure 5 a). The same reader thus distinguishes models that appear equivalent when judged only by their final answers.

sections.heading: Complementary clues enable joint recovery.
sections.text: Complete recovery from the pool, but not any singleton or the query alone, occurs in 14/200 Native-only versus 3/200 ACU cases; raw-content audits identify complementary evidence in 10 and 2 cases, respectively. In ten Native-only cases with complementary evidence, deleting key clues leaves 1/10 complete recoveries, versus 9/10 after equal-length irrelevant deletions (Table F.7 ). Equal-length controls tie this drop to the deleted clues, providing direct evidence for the compositional failure in Section 3.1 .

sections.heading: Reconstruction targets how messages are used.
sections.text: On 60 matched questions, ACU lowers raw-message factual support from 40.3% to 27.7% alongside lower reader recovery (Table F.1 ). This audit supports reduced factual disclosure independently of reader behavior. Semantic-direct further matches views, weighting, utility protection, and training budget. Across three paired runs, reconstruction lowers Full ROUGE by 3.8 pp and factual coverage by 3.1 pp on average (Appendix F.6 ). These matched controls support the benefit of reconstruction feedback beyond direct semantic scoring. Figure 4 b then compares each training variant across native final, best-singleton, joint, and Full views. This comparison tests whether an objective mainly suppresses the delivered answer or also reduces evidence available elsewhere in the interaction. Singleton-only training leaves 29.6% Full recovery. Together, these controls support learning from the downstream use of pooled evidence. We next separate the components that turn this feedback into effective unlearning.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: In this paper, we show that shared-model teams expose forgotten knowledge missed by final-answer evaluations. Our theoretical analysis reveals how complementary messages enable recovery, motivating a multi-view recovery objective. We propose ACU , which uses reconstruction feedback and message-level credit assignment to reduce recoverable evidence while preserving utility. Experiments on TOFU and WMDP-bio show effective forgetting, with gains under matched training budgets and no extra inference calls. We believe this work advances robust LLM unlearning and team safety toward more trustworthy collaboration.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: While ACU improves robustness to collaboration, three limitations remain. (1) Training cost: reconstruction and replacement rollouts add computation, which can limit scalability. (2) Evaluation scope: two benchmarks and fixed audits do not cover adaptive recovery or longer interactions. (3) Measurement: recovery depends on readers and metrics, and does not establish parameter-level deletion. Future work will explore cheaper feedback and broader evaluations of collaborative forgetting.

sections.heading: Ethical Considerations
sections.text: This research is conducted with a strong commitment to ethical and responsible LLM development. Our experiments use public benchmarks, including TOFU’s fictional biographies and WMDP-bio, under controlled evaluation protocols. Recovery audits serve to identify and mitigate information leakage from collaborative models. Recovery procedures could also be misused to reconstruct private or hazardous information. Moreover, overreliance on favorable audit scores may obscure residual leakage, motivating broader evaluation before sensitive deployment. We aim to strengthen forgetting while preserving useful capabilities, supporting safer deployment of LLM teams. We advocate using these methods to respect privacy and reduce harmful information exposure.

sections.text: The recovery update can be implemented with a scalar surrogate. Its gradient is the weighted replacement estimator in Equation C.2 ; minibatches average these contributions. Each audit uses the actions of its corresponding direct or collaborative trajectory. The log probabilities are evaluated on the original sampled actions. Replacement trajectories provide baseline scores, rather than additional action terms in this estimator. For example, replacing a proposer requires regenerating the remaining execution suffix so that the aggregator sees the replacement message. Replacing the aggregator keeps all proposals fixed and generates a new final answer. These two branches compare different decisions under their respective prefixes, even though both update the same adapter. The scalar feedback is fixed during backpropagation, allowing ordinary gradient accumulation across roles without backpropagating through either generated text or the frozen reader. The retained-data terms are then added with the signs in Equation C.2 . Cross-entropy encourages retained answers, while a positive utility multiplier increases the incentive to improve the corresponding direct or team score. Holding the policy snapshot fixed during rollout collection ensures that original actions, replacements, and likelihoods refer to the same model. After optimization, trajectories are refreshed.

sections.heading: F.11 Connecting the mechanism audits
sections.text: The supplementary analyses examine successive parts of the same recovery process: what evidence a team emits, how a reader combines it, and whether the resulting improvement transfers across evaluation settings. Holding the reader fixed while changing its input isolates the contribution of the generated messages. The lower recovery from ACU trajectories therefore supports an effect on the information exposed by the team, beyond the behavior of its native final answer. Paired joint-only events identify questions for which combining messages changes the recovery outcome. A failed singleton answer, however, need not mean that its message lacks the relevant fact. The content inspection separates complementary evidence from cases where the reader overlooks an already sufficient message. Removing an essential fragment and comparing with an irrelevant-fragment deletion then tests whether the identified evidence contributes to joint recovery. These checks give the paired events a more specific interpretation than aggregate score differences alone. The incomplete-recovery and matched-question audits address a different question: whether ACU reduces the target facts supported by the emitted text. The former describes each model’s selected failure cases; the latter compares both models on the same questions, making the content contrast directly paired. Read alongside the fixed-reader control, they support the proposed mechanism of reducing evidence available for reconstruction. Finally, held-out readers and matched-call protocols test whether the advantage persists when reconstruction or generation changes. This progression connects the observed collaboration gap to the training objective, then checks its consequences beyond the primary reader and team configuration.

sections.heading: Relating the outcome measures.
sections.text: Native UE asks whether the deployed model still produces the designated answer, whereas recovery evaluates what a separate reader can reconstruct from the accessible messages. Their different access patterns are central to the collaboration gap: a native refusal can coexist with useful fragments in the transcript. Within recovery evaluation, ROUGE measures lexical overlap and factual coverage measures recovery of the annotated target facts. A reconstruction can therefore change in wording without losing the same amount of factual content. Reading these scores together helps distinguish less direct repetition from less recoverable evidence. WMDP-bio contributes a separate test of native multiple-choice forgetting and retained capability; the detailed message-recovery analyses use TOFU. Together, the recovery audits link ACU ’s advantage to reduced exposure of usable evidence during collaboration. Reconstruction feedback trains the shared model to address this gap, while deployment preserves the original team protocol without reader or replacement calls.

Robust Unlearning for Shared-Model LLM Teams Fudan Institute on Networking Systems of AI Abstract LLM unlearning is essential for removing sensitive or unwanted knowledge while preserving useful capabilities. As LLM teams are increasingly used to solve complex problems, forgetting must remain effective during collaboration. Despite advances in forgetting effectiveness, efficiency, and robustness to relearning, team deployment remains underexplored. We find that collaboration weakens forgetting: final-answer evaluations miss recoverable evidence in team messages, including complementary clues supporting joint recovery. We establish theoretically and confirm empirically that controlling final answers or individual messages does not ensure low recovery from their combination. To address this challenge, we propose Aggregation-Conditioned Unlearning ( ACU ). ACU trains a shared model using reconstruction feedback from individual and pooled messages, prioritizes views with higher recovery risk, and uses replacement-based credit assignment while protecting direct and collaborative utility. TOFU evaluates trajectory-level recovery, while WMDP-bio tests native forgetting and retained utility. On TOFU, ACU lowers full-trajectory recovery from 41.8% to 19.3% in ROUGE-L recall and factual recovery from 34.2% to 18.7% versus output-supervised training, with comparable retained-task performance. These results demonstrate that ACU curbs information leakage in LLM teams and generalizes across team sizes and readers. 1 Introduction LLM teams are increasingly used to solve complex problems by comparing perspectives ( Du et al., 2023 ) , sharing evidence ( Wu et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2023b ; Hong et al., 2023 ) , and combining partial solutions ( Jiang et al., 2023 ; Wang et al., 2025b ; Li et al., 2025 ) . Commercial systems such as GPT-5 pro and Grok 4 Heavy likewise use parallel reasoning to improve performance on difficult tasks ( OpenAI, 2025 ; xAI, 2025 ) . Alongside this growing use, LLM unlearning provides a way to remove unwanted knowledge while preserving useful capabilities ( Shi et al., 2024 ) . Its applications include reducing toxic behavior, removing copyrighted or private information, and limiting access to hazardous knowledge ( Yao et al., 2024 ; Eldan and Russinovich, 2023 ; Li et al., 2024 ; Barez et al., 2025 ) . Their combined use calls for teams that retain useful capabilities while respecting what their models have been trained to forget. Figure 1 : Unlearning under collaboration with fixed weights. (a) Complementary clues reveal a target despite refusal. (b) Direct/team native forget ROUGE (%); annotations: team-minus-direct gaps (pp). Early LLM unlearning methods focused on improving forgetting effectiveness and efficiency. Gradient-based updates suppress designated knowledge without retraining from scratch ( Bărbulescu and Triantafillou, 2024 ) , while preference-based methods such as NPO and SimNPO improve the balance between forgetting and retention ( Jang et al., 2022 ; Zhang et al., 2024a ; Fan et al., 2024a ) . Subsequent work has broadened the focus to robustness: forgotten knowledge may reappear after further fine-tuning, adversarial prompting, or repeated querying ( Lynch et al., 2024 ; Łucki et al., 2024 ; Deeb and Roger, 2024 ) . Recent approaches therefore strengthen resistance to relearning and train against knowledge recoverable through additional generations ( Fan et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025a ; Reisizadeh et al., 2026 ) . Although these advances strengthen unlearning under challenging conditions, they leave a deployment question unresolved: does forgetting survive when unlearned models collaborate as a team? Wider team deployment makes this question increasingly urgent. Collaboration turns one model response into evidence for another, allowing incomplete disclosures to combine into a forgotten answer. Figure 1 (a) presents an independent leakage case: a direct query receives a refusal, yet clues about an email’s format, identity, and domain reveal the address together. The excerpts and role labels highlight disclosed content (Appendix D.1 ). Figure 1 (b) shows the broader effect: all evaluated conventional methods expose more target knowledge under team deployment. We study shared-model teams whose proposers and aggregator reuse the same unlearned weights, fixed throughout inference. We establish theoretically and verify empirically that controlling final answers or individual messages does not ensure low recovery from their combination. Thus, robust collaborative unlearning must address what messages enable others to recover . To address the above challenges, we propose Aggregation-Conditioned Unlearning ( ACU ) , which trains the shared model to reduce recovery from its collaborative interactions. Its design has three parts. First, a frozen reader reconstructs targets from individual and pooled messages, exposing information missed by answer-only supervision. Second, risk-based weighting prioritizes the most revealing views, while replacement-based credit assignment compares alternative messages to guide updates. Third, utility constraints protect useful responses in both direct and team deployment. Together, these components form a generate–reconstruct–update loop that trains against downstream disclosure while preserving the benefits of collaboration. We evaluate ACU on TOFU and WMDP-bio across Llama, Qwen, and Gemma models, varying team size, message access, readers, and training budgets. On TOFU, ACU reduces full-trajectory recovery from 41.8% to 19.3% in ROUGE-L recall and factual recovery from 34.2% to 18.7% versus output-supervised training, with comparable retained-task performance. Content audits and ablations support the analysis by linking these gains to reduced message disclosure and the recovery objective. Transfer to larger teams and unseen readers demonstrates that ACU mitigates collaborative leakage beyond its training configuration. Briefly put, our key contributions are summarized as follows: • Problem discovery. We identify collaboration as a failure mode of LLM unlearning and establish, through theory and experiments, why suppressing individual or final answers can leave forgotten knowledge recoverable from the team’s combined messages. • Practical solution. We propose ACU , a framework that turns reconstruction across message views into training feedback, combining risk prioritization, replacement-based credit assignment, and utility constraints to reduce collaborative leakage while retaining useful capabilities. • Experimental evaluation. Evaluations on two benchmarks and three model families show that ACU reduces TOFU full-trajectory recovery from 41.8% to 19.3% and factual recovery from 34.2% to 18.7% at comparable utility, with transfer across teams and readers. 2 Related Work Figure 2 : Overview of ACU. Team generation, multi-view reconstruction, and utility-preserving updates train the shared model for collaborative deployment. Robust Unlearning. LLM unlearning designs targeted parameter updates to remove designated knowledge, with effectiveness assessed through forgetting, retained utility, and privacy ( Yao et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2024 ; Shi et al., 2024 ) . Robustness research extends this goal to subsequent model use: relearning-resistant methods stabilize forgetting after further training ( Fan et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025a ) , while recovery-aware methods address repeated and multi-turn queries ( Reisizadeh et al., 2026 ; Pan and Wang, 2026 ) . These approaches leave message exchange among unlearned teammates unaddressed. Team Safety. Agent safety examines how memory poisoning ( Chen et al., 2024 ) , infectious jailbreaks ( Gu et al., 2024 ) , agent profiles, and communication topology ( Zhang et al., 2024b ; Yu et al., 2024 ) shape unsafe behavior. Privacy defenses address combined disclosures ( Patil et al., 2025 ) , while ALU and Agentic Unlearning address inference-time removal and parameter–memory backflow, respectively ( Sanyal and Mandal, 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) . Yet preserving learned forgetting during team message exchange remains an open training problem. Team Learning. Team learning improves individual policies using collective feedback, through centralized optimization ( Lowe et al., 2017 ; Yu et al., 2022 ) and coordination in networked systems ( Song et al., 2022 ; Qian et al., 2026 ; Jin et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2023a ) . For LLM teams, Stronger-MAS learns from task rewards; C3 assigns credit through message replacements ( Zhao et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026 ) . Building on these ideas, ACU is, to our knowledge, the first to optimize shared-model unlearning against downstream recovery from collaborative message views. 3 Methodology Figure 2 outlines ACU ’s generate–reconstruct–update loop. The shared model first produces a team interaction; a frozen reader then tests what forgotten knowledge its messages reveal. Recovery feedback guides the next model update, together with feedback on retained tasks. Section 3.1 defines the collaborative unlearning problem, Section 3.2 turns message recovery into an objective, and Section 3.3 explains how to optimize that objective through message-level credit assignment. We combine the weighted recovery gradients with retained cross-entropy and separate direct/team utility penalties (Equation C.2 ). Each penalty multiplier increases when its utility falls below the corresponding threshold (Equation A.14 ), strengthening the incentive to recover useful behavior. Proposal views supervise proposers; native team-final and Full views also supervise aggregation. All role gradients accumulate in the same model, so both evidence generation and its synthesis can improve. After each update, ACU regenerates interactions to reflect the changed model. Validation selects the feasible model with the lowest maximum mean audit risk (Equation 3 ). Algorithm 1 in Appendix C gives the full procedure. This completes the loop: training uses readers and replacements to improve forgetting, while deployment retains the original team protocol and its four target-model calls. 4 Experiments 4.1 Experimental Setup Tasks and Benchmarks. TOFU ( Maini et al., 2024 ) tests forgetting of fictional biographies under forget10/retain90, with 200 held-out forget questions; WMDP-bio ( Li et al., 2024 ) tests hazardous-knowledge removal. We measure native and reader-based exposure using ROUGE-L recall ( Lin, 2004 ) and factual coverage R R , excluding question-provided facts. Retain ROUGE, MMLU ( Hendrycks et al., 2020 ) , and benign refusal (BR) assess useful capability. In Table 1 , Team-final and Retain denote native team forget and retain ROUGE, respectively. Scores are percentages; differences use percentage points (pp). Baselines. GA, WGA, SalUn, DPO, NPO, SimNPO, and CEU cover gradient-, preference-, and constraint-based unlearning (Appendix E ). To isolate supervision, Native-only scores direct/team-final answers, Direct-message scores raw proposals, and Semantic-direct assesses semantic support in ACU ’s views. RULE-GradDiff tests forget-data augmentation; retain-only retraining provides a deletion reference. Implementation Details. Teams use Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, or Gemma-2-9B ( Grattafiori et al., 2024 ; Qwen et al., 2024 ; Gemma Team et al., 2024 ) . The default has three proposers and an aggregator; frozen Qwen reconstructs once per view with greedy decoding and a 96-token cap. The mixed team’s direct reference is its Qwen aggregator. We optimize rank-16 shared LoRA adapters with AdamW at 10 − 5 10^{-5} on two A100 80GB GPUs. Training comparisons use an 18 GPU-hour cap including feedback and validation. Conventional methods expose more knowledge in teams: Llama SimNPO’s forget ROUGE rises from 16.2% to 28.6% (Table 1 ). ACU reaches 12.5%, below GA’s 18.2%, while retaining 55.6% versus 39.1% team ROUGE. Across all four team configurations, ACU reduces team-final exposure by 15.7–16.7 pp and improves team retain by 1.9–4.8 pp over SimNPO. Forgetting thus improves while preserving the useful collaboration that motivates team deployment. The advantage extends to recovered knowledge. Full-trajectory recovery reaches 19.3% with ACU , versus 41.8% for Native-only, 28.7% for Direct-message, 23.1% for Semantic-direct, and 32.6% for RULE-GradDiff (Table F.1 ). Against Native-only, factual recovery falls from 34.2% to 18.7%, with direct/team retain each differing by only 0.2 pp. Benign refusal also falls from 25.4% to 5.2%, supporting selective forgetting rather than general suppression of useful responses. On WMDP-bio’s native multiple-choice test, ACU reaches 27.9% forget accuracy (25% chance) while retaining 65.4% MMLU (Table 2 ). Deployment changes preserve the advantage. Larger teams increase exposure, yet at seven proposers ACU gives 25.0% Full recovery versus Native-only’s 49.4% (Figure 4 a). Qwen targets give 22.1% versus 45.2% (Table F.2 ); held-out Mistral readers give 21.4% versus 45.0% (Figure 5 b). Reader transfer uses fixed trajectories, isolating generalization beyond the training reader. Repeat, Paraphrase, Roles, and Roles+aggregation all favor ACU with four target calls and one reader call under common token allowances (Figure 5 c). These gains motivate examining what changes in the messages themselves. 4.3 Mechanism Analysis Final answers miss recoverable evidence. With the Qwen reader, prompt, and budget fixed, final-answer-only recovery is nearly identical for Native-only and ACU : 14.7% versus 14.9%. Adding proposals raises recovery by 27.1 versus 4.4 pp, exposing a 22.5 pp gap (Figure 5 a). The same reader thus distinguishes models that appear equivalent when judged only by their final answers. Complementary clues enable joint recovery. Dashed tails retain the scores of completed runs. 5 Conclusion In this paper, we show that shared-model teams expose forgotten knowledge missed by final-answer evaluations. Our theoretical analysis reveals how complementary messages enable recovery, motivating a multi-view recovery objective. We propose ACU , which uses reconstruction feedback and message-level credit assignment to reduce recoverable evidence while preserving utility. Experiments on TOFU and WMDP-bio show effective forgetting, with gains under matched training budgets and no extra inference calls. We believe this work advances robust LLM unlearning and team safety toward more trustworthy collaboration. Limitations While ACU improves robustness to collaboration, three limitations remain. (1) Training cost: reconstruction and replacement rollouts add computation, which can limit scalability. (2) Evaluation scope: two benchmarks and fixed audits do not cover adaptive recovery or longer interactions. (3) Measurement: recovery depends on readers and metrics, and does not establish parameter-level deletion. Future work will explore cheaper feedback and broader evaluations of collaborative forgetting. Ethical Considerations This research is conducted with a strong commitment to ethical and responsible LLM development. Our experiments use public benchmarks, including TOFU’s fictional biographies and WMDP-bio, under controlled evaluation protocols. Recovery audits serve to identify and mitigate information leakage from collaborative models. Recovery procedures could also be misused to reconstruct private or hazardous information. Moreover, overreliance on favorable audit scores may obscure residual leakage, motivating broader evaluation before sensitive deployment. We aim to strengthen forgetting while preserving useful capabilities, supporting safer deployment of LLM teams. We advocate using these methods to respect privacy and reduce harmful information exposure.
